(RCE) to complete the second verification of the REDD+ Project in the Alto Huayabamba  Conservation Concession (CCAH) for the reporting period from January 1st, 2019, to December  31st, 2020.   The REDD+ Project in the Alto Huayabamba Conservation Concession (Project) is a project  which seeks to reduce the emission of greenhouse gases (GHG) by implementing four strategic  lines:  (1)  suitable  production;  (2)  environmental  education  and  training;  (3)  organization  and  governance; and (4) controlling migration.   The goal of this GHG emissions inventory verification is to ensure that the GHG assertion is  materially correct, that the data provided to RCE can be documented and if errors or omissions  are detected, they be corrected. The scope of the verification included the assessment of the  Project Description (PD), the Monitoring Report and supporting data and documentation against  the requirements of the VCS Program Guide, Version 4.0 and the VCS Standard, Version 4.1,  CCB Standard and Rules v. 2.0, as well as the project methodology, VM0015 Methodology for  Avoided Unplanned Deforestation, version 1.1 (Methodology).   The  verification  audit  was  performed  through  a  combination  of  document  review,  interviews  with relevant personnel and on-site inspections. During the verification process, RCE issued  three  rounds  of  findings  including  1  Corrective  Action  Request,  2  additional  documentation  requests and 3 clarification requests. The findings are included as Appendix A. RCE concludes,  to a reasonable level of assurance, that the Project correctly applies the Methodology with noted  deviations. RCE confirms, to a reasonable level of assurance, that the Project’s assertion for  the second reporting period of 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2020, is 113,177 tCO2e net  emission reductions, which after applying discounts corresponds to 92,467 claimable VCUs. | :

:  | : South Pole Carbon Asset Management S.A.S. (SP) contracted Ruby Canyon Environmental,  Inc. (RCE) to complete the second verification of the REDD+ Project in the Alto Huayabamba  Conservation Concession (CCAH) for the reporting period from January 1st, 2019, to December  31st, 2020.   The REDD+ Project in the Alto Huayabamba Conservation Concession (Project) is a project  which seeks to reduce the emission of greenhouse gases (GHG) by implementing four strategic  lines:  (1)  suitable  production;  (2)  environmental  education  and  training;  (3)  organization  and  governance; and (4) controlling migration.   The goal of this GHG emissions inventory verification is to ensure that the GHG assertion is  materially correct, that the data provided to RCE can be documented and if errors or omissions  are detected, they be corrected. The scope of the verification included the assessment of the  Project Description (PD), the Monitoring Report and supporting data and documentation against  the requirements of the VCS Program Guide, Version 4.0 and the VCS Standard, Version 4.1,  CCB Standard and Rules v. 2.0, as well as the project methodology, VM0015 Methodology for  Avoided Unplanned Deforestation, version 1.1 (Methodology).   The  verification  audit  was  performed  through  a  combination  of  document  review,  interviews  with relevant personnel and on-site inspections. Benefits of Biodiversity:  The project area contains significant concentrations of fauna and flora  with local, regional, national and global importance. At least 15  endemic species of fauna have been identified, 12 of which are  considered under threat by the Union for Conservation of Nature  (IUCN, These species include: three species of primate, two of  which—the Andean night monkey (Aotus miconax [EN]) and the  yellow-tailed woolly monkey (Lagothrix flavicauda [CR]), currently the  most threatened primate species in Peru—are endemic to Peruvian  forests, whilst the white-bellied spider monkey (Ateles belzebuth [EN])  is also native elsewhere; eight endemic species of birds, one of which  is categorised as near-threatened (Leptopogon taczanowskii), one as  vulnerable (Grallaria przewalskii) and two as endangered  (Aulacorhynchus huallagae and Poecilotriccus luluae); five endemic  species of amphibians and reptiles, one of which has been  categorised as endangered (Noblella lynchi) and three of which have  had their known range expanded as they had not previously been  reported in the area; and four big mammals, two of which are  classified as near-threatened (Nasuella olivacea and Cuniculus  taczanowskii) and two as vulnerable (Leopardus tigrinus and Pudu  mephistopheles).  In terms of flora, no endemic species have been recorded to date, but  a few rare species have been observed: Semiramisia speciosa  (Ericaceae) and Bonnetia paniculata (Bonnetiaceae), of which there  are very few records and samples collected in Peru, alongside what is  potentially a new species—a palm of the genus Ceroxylon sp.—which  is thought to differ from the rest of the species currently known within  this genus.  The conservation of the CCAH forest and the biodiversity that inhabits  it has been made possible by the quest to provide sustainable  livelihoods for resident communities both within and outside of the  concession. Between 2013 and 2020, the deforestation of 799  hectares of Peruvian yungas were avoided, 245 of which were  reduced during this monitoring period. Benefits of Biodiversity:  The project area contains significant concentrations of fauna and flora  with local, regional, national and global importance. At least 15 endemic  species of fauna have been identified, 12 of which are considered under  threat by the Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN, These species  include:  three  species  of  primate,  two  of  which—the  Andean  night  monkey  (Aotus  miconax  [EN])  and  the  yellow-tailed  woolly  monkey  (Lagothrix  flavicauda  [CR]),  currently  the  most  threatened  primate  species  in  Peru—are  endemic  to  Peruvian  forests,  whilst  the  white- bellied spider monkey (Ateles belzebuth [EN]) is also native elsewhere;  eight  endemic species  of  birds,  one  of  which  is categorised  as  near- threatened  (Leptopogon  taczanowskii),  one  as  vulnerable  (Grallaria  przewalskii)  and  two  as  endangered  (Aulacorhynchus  huallagae  and  Poecilotriccus luluae); five endemic species of amphibians and reptiles,  one of which has been categorised as endangered (Noblella lynchi) and  three of which have had their known range expanded as they had not  previously  been  reported  in  the  area;  and  four  big  mammals,  two  of  which  are  classified  as  near-threatened  (Nasuella  olivacea  and  Cuniculus taczanowskii) and two as vulnerable (Leopardus tigrinus and  Pudu mephistopheles).  In terms of flora, no endemic species have been recorded to date, but  a  few  rare  species  have  been  observed:  Semiramisia  speciosa  (Ericaceae) and Bonnetia paniculata (Bonnetiaceae), of which there are  very  few  records  and  samples  collected  in  Peru,  alongside  what  is  potentially a new species—a palm of the genus Ceroxylon sp.—which  is thought to differ from the rest of the species currently known within  this genus.  The conservation of the CCAH forest and the biodiversity that inhabits  it  has  been  made  possible  by  the  quest  to  provide  sustainable  livelihoods  for  resident  communities  both  within  and  outside  of  the  concession.  Since  the  project  starting  date,  the  deforestation  of  900  hectares of Peruvian yungas was avoided, 101 of which were reduced  during this monitoring period.
